title: Why ZM Stock Prints So Much Cash Right Now
detail:
Why ZM Stock Prints So Much Cash Right Now
Trefis Team
Fri, August 28, 2026 at 4:17 PM MDT 4 min read
ZM
MSFT
CRM
CSCO
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by Luca Sammarco on Pexels

The video-call giant is generating far more cash than the average company, yet the market is treating it like a business in decline. Here's the offer on the table.

The market is offering a cash machine at a discount, which raises the central question for any investor: is this a high-yield bargain, or is the market correctly pricing in a future breakdown?

The cash flow is built on a profitable, expanding platform. Zoom (ZM)'s ability to generate cash is not a recent fluke. The company has produced positive free cash flow in every twelve-month period for the last three years, totaling $1.93 billion in the most recent stretch. This is the output of a highly profitable operation, with a trailing operating margin of 24%, well above the 18.5% S&P 500 median. The balance sheet is also clean, with net cash of about $7.2 billion, meaning the high yield isn't an illusion created by debt. The machine behind these numbers is Zoom's strategic shift from a single-product application to an integrated communications platform.

While revenue growth of 5.0% over the last year trails the 8.3% median for large companies, management is focused on selling a broader "AI-first system of action." This includes products like Zoom Phone and Zoom Contact Center, which are driving larger, multi-year deals with corporate clients. The market is pricing a gap between new wins and existing customer spend. The offer exists because the market sees a contradiction in Zoom's story. On one hand, the push into the enterprise is showing clear results. Enterprise revenue recently grew 7.8%, its strongest rate in three years. The company's remaining performance obligations, which represent future contracted revenue, jumped 14% to $4.5 billion, signaling success in landing bigger commitments.

But there is a catch. The company's trailing 12-month net dollar expansion rate for enterprise customers was 99%. In simple terms, for every dollar Zoom received from its existing enterprise clients a year ago, it now gets 99 cents. Upsells and cross-sells are being slightly offset by churn and downgrades. This creates a difficult situation where growth depends heavily on winning new customers, because the current base isn't expanding its spend. Compounding this, management's latest outlook assumes "flat online growth," putting the full weight of the company's future on that enterprise segment. The entire offer hinges on turning new platform deals into net expansion. The debate over Zoom's value boils down to this tension. The company is a cash-rich, highly profitable business that is successfully winning larger deals with new enterprise customers. Yet it has not yet proven it can consistently expand spending within its existing customer base.

title: Has Microsoft Stock Run Ahead Of Its AI Payoff?

Has Microsoft Stock Run Ahead Of Its AI Payoff?

Image by Pexels from Pixabay

The software giant's stock has a powerful business engine behind its long-term trend, but a rapid run-up back toward all-time highs forces investors to ask if the price of admission is still worth paying.

Microsoft (MSFT) has built one of the most durable cash-generation engines in enterprise technology, but its stock currently trades about 6% below its 52-week high. For any investor sizing up the company's dominant push into artificial intelligence, the central question is clear: is this a consolidation pause before another leg higher, or has the current price already captured the payoff? While the stock's broader trend strength ranks near the middle of US-listed stocks above $1B, the recent rally to within 6% of its 52-week high brings the core tension into focus: does the fundamental engine justify the elevated valuation?

The core investment case rests on this underlying operational momentum rather than technical strength, raising the question of whether the current price offers sufficient upside for new buyers.

Is This a Genuine Business Surge?

The numbers behind Microsoft's run are strong. The company's operating margin over the last twelve months is a huge 47%, far outpacing the S&P 500 median of 18.5%. This isn't a one-time event; its three-year average is similarly high. Revenue growth tells the same story, at 17.8% over the past year, more than double the 8.3% median for the index.

This financial power comes directly from its strategic execution in AI and cloud computing. In its most recent quarter, revenue from Azure and other cloud services grew 43%, a clear sign that demand for its AI services is intense. Management confirmed that "Customer demand continues to exceed available capacity." The adoption of its AI tools is also rapid, with the company reporting it now has "over 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats."

What Does a Share of This Engine Cost?

The market is well aware of this operational strength, and it charges a premium. Microsoft trades at a price-to-earnings multiple of 28.0, compared to an S&P 500 median of 23.3. That premium exists even after a stretch of relative underperformance: over the trailing twelve months, Microsoft has been largely flat, trailing the S&P 500's +21% return. The stock also trades about 6% below its two-year high of $537.65, reinforcing that buyers today are not chasing a fresh peak.

The primary risk centers on the sheer scale of capital expenditure required to sustain this AI buildout. Some analysts are asking if soaring capital expenditures could put the stock's valuation at risk. The concern is that the company is building for a level of demand that might not materialize, or that rising component costs could squeeze profitability. This risk is compounded by declines in legacy businesses. Management expects revenue from its Windows OEM and Devices segment to "decline in the high teens for the fiscal year," and Xbox revenue recently decreased 10%. For investors who prefer broader exposure to the technology sector without concentrating on a single company's execution risk, a technology ETF like VGT might be an alternative.

title: Is Adobe Stock’s AI Strategy Worth The Near-Term Risk?
detail:
Is Adobe Stock’s AI Strategy Worth The Near-Term Risk?
Trefis Team

Image by Pexels from Pixabay

A creative software titan is trading at a steep discount, but a major strategy shift has investors wondering if the price is a bargain or a breakdown.

Adobe (ADBE) is the architecture of the modern creative and business world, the company behind Photoshop, Premiere, and the ubiquitous PDF. Yet the market has put a surprisingly low price on this franchise. After a significant markdown, the stock trades at a price-to-earnings multiple of 16.1, a steep discount to the S&P 500 median of 23.3. That kind of gap on a household name forces a question every bargain hunter must answer: is this discount a buying opportunity, or does it reflect market skepticism over slowing growth?

How can a business this profitable be this cheap?

By the numbers, Adobe looks less like a company in trouble and more like a fortress. Its operating margin over the last twelve months was 36%, nearly double the S&P 500 median of 18.5%. This isn't a stagnant business, either; revenue grew 11.5% over the same period, outpacing the broader market.

More importantly, the earnings are backed by cash, and lots of it. The company's operating cash flow margin is a huge 42%, a clear sign of a high-quality, capital-light business model. The fundamentals paint a picture of a dominant enterprise that converts a huge portion of its sales directly into cash. This is the core of the value argument: a highly profitable, growing, cash-generating leader trading well below the market average.

Is a strategic pivot the real reason for the discount?

The value-trap screen found just one flaw: operating margin shrank by a slight 0.3 percentage points over the last year. But the market's real anxiety isn't about that sliver of margin; it's about a deliberate, high-stakes pivot in strategy. Management recently announced a plan to aggressively pursue a "freemium" model for its AI-powered products like Firefly, prioritizing user acquisition over immediate sales. This shift comes at a cost.

Management stated the move "lowers our second half ARR growth expectations from individual subscribers" and involves a decision to "defer previously planned Creative Cloud second half line optimizations." In short, Adobe is trading predictable, high-margin revenue for a long-term bet on converting a large new user base. This strategic gamble is happening during a leadership transition, with an active CEO search underway and an interim CFO in place, adding a layer of execution risk. An investor might wonder what the market's discount is really pricing in, given these moving parts. For those who prefer to invest in the sector as a whole, a broader software ETF like IGV offers an alternative to single-stock risk.

S&P 500 Posts Slight Weekly Gain as Tech Earnings Top Expectations

^GSPC

CRWD

Trading disclosure

The Standard & Poor's 500 index edged up 0.5% this week amid stronger-than-expected quarterly reports from tech companies including Salesforce (CRM) and CrowdStrike (CRWD).

The S&P 500 ended the week at 7,711.76. With just one session remaining in the month, the market benchmark is up 3% for August and has climbed 13% this year.

At the annual Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh reaffirmed his commitment to the Fed's mandates, including the 2% inflation goal. Warsh said inflation numbers were concerning, citing the Fed's preferred metric -- the personal consumption expenditure price index -- which was unchanged at 3.7% year over year in July.

Data released earlier this week showed US economic growth, measured by gross domestic product, rose by 1.5% in Q2. This was unrevised from the advance estimate released last month and matched expectations in a survey compiled by Bloomberg.

The University of Michigan consumer sentiment index was revised upward on Friday to 51.7 for August from 51.0 in the preliminary estimate, compared with expectations for no revision in a survey compiled by Bloomberg. The latest reading was still below July's final print of 55.2.

The technology sector had the largest percentage increase this week, climbing 1.8%, followed by a 1.6% advance in communication services and a 1.1% rise in financials. Consumer discretionary eked out a 0.1% gain.

Salesforce was the best performer in both the technology sector and the overall S&P 500 this week, jumping 22%. The company reported fiscal Q2 adjusted earnings and revenue above analysts' mean estimates and boosted its fiscal 2027 guidance.

CrowdStrike had the second-largest percentage gain in technology and the overall S&P 500, climbing 14%. The company reported better-than-expected fiscal second-quarter results. CrowdStrike also raised its guidance for full-year net new annual recurring revenue, or ARR, amid increasing demand for cybersecurity solutions to address artificial intelligence risks.

The health care and energy sectors fell 2% each, followed by a 1.7% decline in industrials and a 1.3% slip in real estate. Consumer staples, materials and utilities also edged lower.

Boston Scientific (BSX) had the largest percentage loss in health care for the week, shedding 7%. The company is recalling thousands of its percutaneous catheters due to possible arterial sheath tip separation that could lead to complications with a retained tip, the US Food and Drug Administration said.

The decline in energy came as crude oil futures also fell on the week. Mediators in the Iran war are stepping up efforts to get the Strait of Hormuz reopened, Reuters reported. Top decliners in the sector included EOG Resources (EOG), which fell 6.3% amid an investment rating downgrade by Capital One to equal weight from overweight.

Earnings reports next week are expected from companies including Palo Alto Networks (PANW), Dell Technologies (DELL), Medtronic (MDT), Broadcom (AVGO) and Snowflake (SNOW).

Investors will be heavily focused on the government's August employment report, due Friday. Other reports will include July construction spending and factory orders.

title: Salesforce (CRM) Stock Soars on Q2 Earnings: Is It Too Late to Buy?
detail:
Salesforce (CRM) Stock Soars on Q2 Earnings: Is It Too Late to Buy?

Salesforce CRM) stock came roaring back after the software giant posted a strong Q2 report after-market hours on Wednesday evening.

CRM shares spiked more than 20% on Thursday, marking their largest single-day jump since 2020, and are up another 3% in Friday's trading session.

The rally reflects renewed confidence that Salesforce can turn artificial intelligence into a growth catalyst rather than be disrupted by AI.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Salesforce Crushes Q2 Earnings & Raises Guidance

Salesforce posted Q2 revenue of $11.34 billion, rising nearly 11% year over year and edging past the Zacks Consensus of $11.31 billion.

More eye-catching was Salesforce's Q2 adjusted net income of $3.53 billion. This translated into adjusted EPS of $5.90, which soared 103% from $2.91 per share a year ago and crushed expectations of $3.27 by more than 80%.

However, it's noteworthy that the enormous EPS beat was heavily boosted by gains on Salesforce's strategic investments, including in artificial intelligence firm Anthropic. Excluding that benefit, underlying adjusted EPS was reportedly around $3.37, which still topped expectations but paints a more realistic picture of operating profitability.

Meanwhile, operating cash flow surged 71% to $1.3 billion and free cash flow jumped 81% to $1.1 billion. Current remaining performance obligations (cRPO), an important indicator of future sales, climbed 14% to $33.5 billion.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

More importantly, management raised its current fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $46.1-$46.4 billion (+11% growth), up from $45.9-$46.2 billion previously, and now forecasts adjusted EPS of $16.67-$16.71 (+33% growth), up from its prior $14.06-$14.12 outlook.

Q3 revenue is expected at $11.42-$11.5 billion, representing an 11%-12% increase.Of course, part of the dramatic full-year EPS increase reflects the strategic investment gains already realized. This makes the higher revenue outlook and sustained 14% cRPO growth arguably more important indicators of Salesforce's underlying momentum, with the current Zacks Consensus sales forecast pictured below.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

AI Momentum Accelerates With Anthropic & Claudeforce

Salesforce's AI story is rapidly becoming measurable through its AI platform Agentforce and its supporting data foundation, Data 360.

Agentforce and Data 360 annual recurring revenue (ARR) reached nearly $3.9 billion, soaring more than 210% YoY, with Agentforce ARR surpassing $1.5 billion and increasing more than 240%.

US equity indexes rose this week as technology-led mega-cap gainers helped outweigh a hotter inflation print and the Trump administration's moves to choke Iran into a peace agreement.

* The S&P 500 closed at 7,711.76 on Friday, up from 7,674.37 a week ago. The Nasdaq Composite stood at about 26,402.42, compared with 26,180.46 a week earlier. The Dow Jones Industrial Average ended at 53,559.99, up from 53,277.01 at the end of last week.

* Nvidia's (NVDA) fiscal Q2 earnings and revenue more than doubled, and Q3 sales forecast beat estimates. The AI bellwether offered a surprisingly strong fiscal 2028 revenue outlook, while its gross margin guidance provided clarity amid rising memory costs, Morgan Stanley said in a note.

* Salesforce (CRM) posted higher fiscal Q2 adjusted earnings and revenue, and lifted its fiscal 2027 guidance.

* CrowdStrike (CRWD) reported surging fiscal Q2 adjusted earnings and sales, and raised its full-year net new annual recurring revenue outlook. This is a "blowout quarter as AI demand inflects across the platform," Truist Securities said.

* The headline personal consumption expenditure price index rose in July, following a slide in June, beating consensus. The annual headline rate exceeded forecast. The Fed's preferred core measure climbed in July, as expected and ahead of the June print. The annual core gauge was steady, as projected.

* The US is targeting aviation, shipping, technology, gold and digital assets to choke off Iran's economy. It is threatening secondary sanctions on countries that refuse to cut economic ties with Tehran. Iran pledged to fight back, expressing confidence that major trading partners would resist this pressure campaign.

* Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh said inflation is the more concerning part of the central bank's dual mandate, recommitting to the 2% inflation goal.
